title: HTTP, HTTPS & DNS
tagline: How browsers turn a URL into pixels — DNS resolution, HTTP request-response, TLS handshake, REST conventions, and WebSockets.

sections.content:
When you type `https://example.com/api/users` and press Enter, a remarkable chain of events unfolds: your OS asks DNS for the IP address, your browser establishes a TCP connection, TLS negotiates encryption, and an HTTP request travels to the server. The response — JSON, HTML, an image — comes back in milliseconds. Every web application is built on this stack.

**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a stateless request-response protocol at Layer 7. **HTTPS** adds TLS (Transport Layer Security) underneath HTTP, encrypting everything so eavesdroppers see only ciphertext. **DNS** (Domain Name System) is the internet's distributed phone book, translating human-readable hostnames into IP addresses. Understanding all three is foundational for building and debugging any web service.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant R as Recursive Resolver
    participant Root as Root Nameserver
    participant TLD as TLD Nameserver
    participant Auth as Authoritative NS
    B->>R: Who is example.com?
    R->>Root: Who handles .com?
    Root->>R: TLD NS for .com
    R->>TLD: Who handles example.com?
    TLD->>R: Authoritative NS for example.com
    R->>Auth: What is the A record for example.com?
    Auth->>R: 93.184.216.34 (TTL 3600)
    R->>B: 93.184.216.34 (cached)
    Note over B,R: Subsequent lookups hit cache until TTL expires
sections.caption: DNS iterative resolution: the resolver queries the hierarchy (root → TLD → authoritative) then caches the answer for TTL seconds.

sections.title: DNS as a Hierarchical Phone Book
sections.content:
Imagine wanting the phone number of 'Alice at Acme Corp'. You call the **Directory Assistance** operator (recursive resolver). They check their notes — not listed. They call the **Country Directory** (root nameserver) who says 'companies in this country use the Business Registry'. They call the **Business Registry** (TLD nameserver for `.com`) who says 'Acme Corp uses its own internal directory'. Finally they call **Acme's internal directory** (authoritative nameserver) and get Alice's number.

The operator writes the number on a sticky note with an expiry time (**TTL**). Next time someone asks for Alice's number, the operator uses the sticky note without repeating the whole chain. This **caching** is why DNS propagation after changing records takes time — old sticky notes haven't expired yet.

**HTTP methods** encode the intended action on a resource. `GET` retrieves (idempotent, no body). `POST` creates or submits (not idempotent). `PUT` replaces a resource completely (idempotent). `PATCH` applies a partial update. `DELETE` removes a resource (idempotent). `HEAD` fetches headers only — useful to check Last-Modified without downloading the body. **Idempotent** means repeating the request has the same effect as one request — crucial for retry logic.

**HTTP status codes** group into five classes: `1xx` informational, `2xx` success (`200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content`), `3xx` redirection (`301 Moved Permanently`, `302 Found`, `304 Not Modified`), `4xx` client errors (`400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized`, `403 Forbidden`, `404 Not Found`, `429 Too Many Requests`), `5xx` server errors (`500 Internal Server Error`, `502 Bad Gateway`, `503 Service Unavailable`). Using correct codes is not ceremonial — clients and proxies make caching and retry decisions based on them.

**HTTPS and TLS**: TLS (v1.3 is current) performs a **handshake** before HTTP data flows: the server sends its certificate (signed by a trusted CA), the client verifies it, they agree on a cipher suite and exchange key material, then all subsequent data is encrypted with symmetric keys. TLS 1.3 reduced the handshake from 2 round trips (TLS 1.2) to **1 round trip** (and 0-RTT resumption for repeat connections). **WebSockets** upgrade an HTTP connection to a persistent full-duplex channel — the client sends an `Upgrade: websocket` header and, after a handshake, both sides can push messages at any time without polling.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    Note over C,S: TLS 1.3 Handshake
    C->>S: ClientHello (ciphers, key_share)
    S->>C: ServerHello + Certificate + Finished
    C->>S: Finished
    Note over C,S: 1 RTT — symmetric keys derived
    C->>S: GET /api/users HTTP/1.1
    S->>C: 200 OK + JSON body
    Note over C,S: All HTTP encrypted inside TLS record
sections.caption: TLS 1.3 handshake needs only 1 round trip before encrypted HTTP can flow, compared to TLS 1.2's 2 RTTs.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: `fetch()` is the modern browser/Node.js (v18+) HTTP API. The critical gotcha: `fetch` only rejects on network failure, not on 4xx/5xx responses — you must check `res.ok` or `res.status`. The WebSocket API is event-driven; once upgraded from HTTP, both client and server can push messages at any time — no polling needed. Use `wss://` (WebSocket over TLS) in production.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Never roll your own TLS** — always use well-maintained libraries (`https` in Node, your cloud load balancer's TLS termination, or a reverse proxy like nginx/Caddy). The practical HTTPS checklist: use TLS 1.2+ (disable 1.0/1.1), enable **HSTS** (`Strict-Transport-Security` header), set short **certificate TTLs** (Let's Encrypt auto-renews every 90 days), and use `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` flags on session cookies. These five steps eliminate the most common HTTPS deployment vulnerabilities.

items: **DNS resolution** follows a hierarchy: recursive resolver → root → TLD nameserver → authoritative nameserver. Results are cached by TTL, which is why DNS changes take time to propagate.
**HTTP methods** encode semantics: GET/HEAD/PUT/DELETE are idempotent; POST creates/triggers and is not. Using correct methods enables correct caching, retry logic, and REST client behaviour.

**Status codes** are load-bearing: `2xx` = success, `3xx` = redirect, `4xx` = client fault (don't retry blindly), `5xx` = server fault (safe to retry with backoff). `fetch()` does not throw on 4xx/5xx — always check `res.ok`.

**TLS 1.3** negotiates encryption in 1 RTT (vs 2 for TLS 1.2) using asymmetric cryptography to agree on symmetric session keys — the certificate proves server identity; all subsequent HTTP is encrypted.
**WebSockets** upgrade an HTTP connection to a persistent full-duplex channel — ideal for live dashboards, chat, and collaborative tools where server-push is needed without polling overhead.

quiz.question: What does the DNS 'TTL' field control?
options: How long the DNS server waits before timing out a query
How long resolvers cache a DNS record before re-querying
The maximum number of DNS servers a query can traverse
The time-to-live for the TLS certificate associated with a domain
quiz.explanation: TTL (Time To Live) in a DNS record specifies how many seconds resolvers and OS caches should keep the answer before re-querying. A TTL of 3600 means caches hold it for 1 hour. Lowering TTL before a planned IP change reduces propagation time.

quiz.question: Which HTTP method is both safe AND idempotent?
options: POST
PUT
DELETE
GET
quiz.explanation: GET is both safe (no side effects, does not modify state) and idempotent (repeating it gives the same result). PUT is idempotent but not safe (it modifies state). POST is neither safe nor idempotent. DELETE is idempotent but not safe.

quiz.question: A client receives HTTP 401. What does this indicate?
options: The resource was not found
The client is authenticated but lacks permission
Authentication is required (or credentials were invalid)
The server encountered an internal error
quiz.explanation: 401 Unauthorized means authentication is required or the provided credentials are invalid. 403 Forbidden means the client IS authenticated but does not have permission to access the resource. 404 is not found; 500 is a server error.

quiz.question: How many round trips does TLS 1.3 require before encrypted data can flow?
options: 0 (0-RTT resumption for new connections)
quiz.explanation: TLS 1.3 requires 1 round trip (ClientHello with key_share → ServerHello + Certificate + Finished → client Finished) before application data flows. TLS 1.2 needed 2 RTTs. 0-RTT is available for resumed sessions but has replay-attack risks.

quiz.question: What HTTP header does a client send to initiate a WebSocket upgrade?
options: Content-Type: websocket
Upgrade: websocket
Protocol-Switch: websocket
Connection: websocket
quiz.explanation: A WebSocket upgrade request includes 'Upgrade: websocket' and 'Connection: Upgrade' headers, plus a 'Sec-WebSocket-Key' nonce. The server responds with 101 Switching Protocols if it accepts the upgrade, then the connection switches to the WebSocket framing protocol.

quiz.question: Which DNS record type is used to map a hostname to an IPv4 address?
options: CNAME
MX
A
TXT
quiz.explanation: An A record maps a hostname to an IPv4 address (e.g., example.com → 93.184.216.34). AAAA maps to IPv6. CNAME is an alias pointing to another hostname. MX specifies mail servers. TXT holds arbitrary text (SPF, DKIM, etc.).

quiz.question: A REST API returns 204. What should the client expect?
options: A JSON object with an empty array
A redirect to the created resource
No response body — the operation succeeded
An error indicating no content was found
quiz.explanation: HTTP 204 No Content means the request succeeded but there is no body to return. It is commonly used for DELETE and PATCH operations where returning the full resource is unnecessary. The client should not try to parse a body.

quiz.question: Why does `fetch()` NOT automatically throw an error on a 404 response?
options: 404 is considered a successful response in the HTTP spec
fetch() only rejects on network-level failures, not HTTP error status codes
fetch() requires a custom error handler plugin to detect 4xx
The response body must be read before the status is available
quiz.explanation: fetch() resolves (not rejects) for any complete HTTP response, even 4xx/5xx. It only rejects on network failures (DNS error, connection refused). You must check res.ok (true for 200-299) or res.status to detect HTTP errors and throw manually.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security)?
options: Encrypting DNS queries to prevent eavesdropping
Instructing browsers to only connect to the site over HTTPS for a specified duration
Requiring two-factor authentication for admin endpoints
Preventing cross-site request forgery attacks
quiz.explanation: The Strict-Transport-Security header tells browsers to always use HTTPS for the domain (and optionally subdomains) for the specified max-age seconds, even if the user types 'http://'. This prevents SSL-stripping attacks where a MITM downgrades to plain HTTP.

quiz.question: In a DNS iterative resolution, which nameserver does the recursive resolver query FIRST?
options: The authoritative nameserver for the domain
The TLD nameserver (e.g., .com servers)
One of the 13 root nameserver clusters
The ISP's local nameserver
quiz.explanation: Iterative resolution starts at the root nameservers (there are 13 root nameserver IP addresses, each operated as an anycast cluster). The root responds with the TLD nameservers (.com, .org, etc.), which in turn respond with the authoritative nameservers for the specific domain.
